text:
1.5 Separating Floor Effect






Important



Luckily, Muthen et al. actually came out with a pretty clever and theoretically meaningful way to address floor effects.
Instead of dropping the floor effect (the lowest value possible), Muthen et al. recommends creating two variables from the original variable. They call this the two-part approach for dealing with floor effects.
Step 1: Create a binary variable.
Create a binary variable that collapses all non-floor scores as 1. Thus, conceptually this variable represents whether a construct is meaingfully occuring or not.
BIN = 0, the construct is not meaningfully occuring. BIN = 1, the construct is meaningfully occuring.
We do loose information about the magnitude of how this construct is taking place, but that’s where part 2 comes in.
Step 2: Create a continuous variable.
In the second step, we code all floor effects as NA (i.e., missing) and retain non-floor effects as original.
Thus, the continous variable is represents what is taking place AFTER removed floor effects which drowned out the variance.
Thus, in analytical models we should include both variables (only possible in SEMs) and allowed to correlate with one another. In doing so, we can understand if a distal variable is related to the occurrence of a construct AND also when it is occurring, the magnitude of that relationship.

2.2.2 Model Specification

pos_ctsem <- "
# Measurement Model
posaff_B =~ esm_pa
posaff_W =~ esm_pa

# Between/Trend
posaff_B  ~  posaff_B     
posaff_B ~~  0*posaff_B # this is what tells model its between-person
posaff_B %~% posaff_B     

# Within (dynamic) factor
posaff_W  ~  posaff_W       
posaff_W ~~  posaff_W       
posaff_W %~% posaff_W       

# CINT
posaff_B ~ 1
"

pos_ctsem_syn <- ct_lavaan(pos_ctsem) 



2.2.3 Fit Model

pos_ctsem_mod <- ctModel(
  type          = "ct",
  id = "id",
  time = "time_day",
  latentNames   = pos_ctsem_syn$latentNames,
  manifestNames = pos_ctsem_syn$manifestNames,
  LAMBDA        = pos_ctsem_syn$LAMBDA,
  DRIFT         = pos_ctsem_syn$DRIFT,
  DIFFUSION     = pos_ctsem_syn$DIFFUSION,
  T0VAR         = pos_ctsem_syn$T0VAR,
  CINT          = pos_ctsem_syn$CINT,
  T0MEANS       = pos_ctsem_syn$T0MEANS,
  MANIFESTMEANS = pos_ctsem_syn$MANIFESTMEANS,
  manifesttype  = pos_ctsem_syn$manifesttype,
  n.TIpred      = 3,
  TIpredNames   = c("zpos", "zneg", "zdis")
)

pos_ctsem_mod$pars[, c("zpos", "zneg", "zdis")] <- FALSE

target <- pos_ctsem_mod$pars$matrix == "DRIFT" &
          pos_ctsem_mod$pars$row    == "posaff_W" &
          pos_ctsem_mod$pars$col    == "posaff_W"

pos_ctsem_mod$pars[target, c("zpos", "zneg", "zdis")] <- TRUE

pos_ctsem_fit <- ctStanFit(
  datalong = p2_data, 
  ctstanmodel = pos_ctsem_mod,
  cores = 10, plot = FALSE, priors = TRUE
)
saveRDS(pos_ctsem_fit, "02_files/pos_ctsem_fit.Rds")

pos_ctsem_fit <- readRDS("02_files/pos_ctsem_fit.Rds")

2.2.5.2 Main Effects

pos_ctsem_fit <- readRDS("02_files/pos_ctsem_fit.Rds")
pos_ctsem_res <- summary(pos_ctsem_fit)
pos_ctsem_res$parmatrices %>%
  filter(matrix == "DRIFT") %>%
  filter(row == col)

  matrix row col   Mean    sd   2.5%    50%  97.5%
1  DRIFT   1   1 -0.032 0.026 -0.107 -0.024 -0.006
2  DRIFT   2   2 -4.296 0.538 -5.399 -4.306 -3.243








Note



The first parameter represents the overall between-person detrend of Positive Affect (-0.03, [-.12, -0.006]). This means that the detrend is fairly weak, and Positive Affect as a “trait” is fairly stable.
The second parameter represents the within-person dynamic return of PA to equilibrium (-4.29 [-5.43, -3.33]). What does this mean practically? This tells us how fast a process returns to equilibrium.
We can actually calculate the half-life using the following:



days <- log(0.5)/-4.29
days

[1] 0.1615728

days*24

[1] 3.877746








Note



Interpretation: For a given deivation from a person’s stable, trait-level positive affect, half of that deviation would dissipate within approximately 3.9 hours–assuming no other force intervened.

  filter(matrix == "dtDRIFT") %>%
  filter(row == col)

Note



When dtDRIFT == 1 (1 day/24 hours), only ~1.6% of the original deviation on PA would remain.





2.2.6 Cross-level Interaction

2.2.6.1 Auto-Effect

pos_ctsem_res$tipreds %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("param") %>%
  filter(grepl("auto_posaff_W", param))

                   param   mean    sd   2.5%    50%  97.5%      z
1 tip_zpos_auto_posaff_W -2.272 0.470 -3.172 -2.268 -1.349 -4.836
2 tip_zneg_auto_posaff_W -1.754 0.397 -2.558 -1.750 -0.992 -4.415
3 tip_zdis_auto_posaff_W  0.809 0.388 -0.004  0.819  1.543  2.084








Note



Similar to the interpretation above, we find significant cross-level interactions. A bigger negative coefficient suggests the time invariant variable predicted faster decay.

Positive Affect (MSS) had the largest negative association (-2.29 [-3.24, -1.35]) with the auto-effect of PA. In other words, greater MSS-PA is associated with a faster decay in within-PA.
Likewise, greater MSS-Negative Affect was also associated with faster decay (-1.76 [-2.61, -0.95]).
However, greater MSS-Disorganized Schitzophrenia was associated with slower decay in PA (0.82 [0.02, 1.59]).





2.2.6.2 Diffusion/Volatility

pos_ctsem_res$tipreds %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("param") %>%
  filter(grepl("diff_posaff_W", param))

                   param   mean    sd   2.5%    50% 97.5%      z
1 tip_zpos_diff_posaff_W  0.410 0.074  0.270  0.408 0.562  5.560
2 tip_zneg_diff_posaff_W  0.291 0.063  0.169  0.290 0.420  4.626
3 tip_zdis_diff_posaff_W -0.113 0.081 -0.274 -0.112 0.045 -1.399








Note



Diffiusion represents the volatility not accounted for by the either the between or wihtin-person AR effects.

MSS-Positive Affect had the largest positive association (0.41 [0.26, 0.57]) the diffusion of within-PA.
Likewise, greater MSS-Negative Affect was also associated with the diffusion of within-PA (0.29 [0.16, 0.41]).
However, greater MSS-Disorganized Schitzophrenia was associated with lower diffusion of within-PA (-0.12 [-0.29, 0.06]); although this was not a credible association.

4.2 Two-Part Approach (Censored Magnitude)

4.2.1 Model Specification

na_twopart_ctsem <- "
# Measurement Model
## BINARY
bin_na_B =~ esm_na_bin
bin_na_W =~ esm_na_bin

## CONT.
con_na_B =~ esm_na_con
con_na_W =~ esm_na_con

# Between/Trend
bin_na_B  ~  bin_na_B
bin_na_B ~~  0*bin_na_B
bin_na_B %~% bin_na_B

con_na_B  ~  con_na_B
con_na_B ~~  0*con_na_B
con_na_B %~% con_na_B

bin_na_B %~% con_na_B

# Within (dynamic) factor
## BINARY
bin_na_W  ~  bin_na_W
bin_na_W ~~  bin_na_W
bin_na_W %~% bin_na_W

## CONT.
con_na_W  ~  con_na_W
con_na_W ~~  con_na_W
con_na_W %~% con_na_W

## T0MEAN
bin_na_B ~t0~ 1
con_na_B ~t0~ 1

BINARY: esm_na_bin
CENSOR: esm_na_con
"

5.2.1 Model Specification

dis_twopart_ctsem <- "
# Measurement Model
## BINARY
bin_dis_B =~ esm_dis_bin
bin_dis_W =~ esm_dis_bin

## CONT.
con_dis_B =~ esm_dis_con
con_dis_W =~ esm_dis_con

# Between/Trend
bin_dis_B  ~  bin_dis_B
bin_dis_B ~~  0*bin_dis_B
bin_dis_B %~% bin_dis_B

con_dis_B  ~  con_dis_B
con_dis_B ~~  0*con_dis_B
con_dis_B %~% con_dis_B

bin_dis_B %~% con_dis_B

# Within (dynamic) factor
## BINARY
bin_dis_W  ~  bin_dis_W
bin_dis_W ~~  bin_dis_W
bin_dis_W %~% bin_dis_W

## CONT.
con_dis_W  ~  con_dis_W
con_dis_W ~~  con_dis_W
con_dis_W %~% con_dis_W

## T0MEAN
bin_dis_B ~t0~ 1
con_dis_B ~t0~ 1

BINARY: esm_dis_bin
CENSOR: esm_dis_con

# Measurement Model
## BINARY

bin_neg3_W =~ esm_neg3_bin

## CONT.

# Between/Trend
bin_neg3_B  ~  bin_neg3_B
bin_neg3_B ~~  0*bin_neg3_B
bin_neg3_B %~% bin_neg3_B

con_neg3_B  ~  con_neg3_B
con_neg3_B ~~  0*con_neg3_B
con_neg3_B %~% con_neg3_B

bin_neg3_B %~% con_neg3_B

# Within (dynamic) factor
## BINARY
bin_neg3_W  ~  bin_neg3_W
bin_neg3_W ~~  bin_neg3_W
bin_neg3_W %~% bin_neg3_W
